rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four real newsroom doors and tells them where each one could collapse. "A writing platform is now asking writers to become video producers" is a sharper human story than B's weaker substitute, "As Substack chases video, the 10% cut becomes the question creators have to answer," which smuggles in an unproven take-rate claim. B is competent, but A is more useful because its proof demands are specific enough to stop a bad pitch before it embarrasses everyone.
gaps_in_A: "Substack has stopped competing with Mailchimp and started competing with YouTube" imports named competitors that were not in the fact block. The strategic frame works, but the headline overclaims.
"the people who chose Substack precisely because it was text now face a feed that rewards something they didn't sign up to make" assumes creator motivation and feed behavior before proving either.
"Video hosting is one of the most expensive infrastructure commitments a platform can make" is plausible, but it needs sourcing; the update only says native video and direct hosting.
gaps_in_B: "the same cut now extending over video and podcast monetization" is the worst sentence in the set. The facts say Substack takes 10% of subscription revenue; they do not say that cut applies identically to video and podcasts.
"short on funding" overstates the supplied fact, which was only that Substack is privately held and has had public funding struggles. That wording implies current distress without evidence.
"no disclosure where disclosure was expected" invents an expectation. The cleaner story is nondisclosure of numerator, denominator, and methodology, not a norm the set has not established.

The set never builds the sharper labor angle; "As Substack chases video, the 10% cut becomes the question creators have to answer" turns creator impact into take-rate math and leaves out the production burden/feed-pressure story.
